【17】In all cases， serial CT scanning documented progressive reso-lution of the clots， most within 1 month after the injury .

【18】Servadei et al. reported a study conducted at 3 Italian neuro-surgical centers involving 158 patients admitted following mi-nor head trauma who had CT evidence of significant extradural hematoma. The size of the hematoma (rather than location) and the degree of midline shift were the factors influential in decision for surgical treatment. Conservative management was utilized for hematomas having a maximum thickness of less than 10 mm with a midline shift of less than 5 mm. Both groups of patients had favorable outcomes in this study .

【19】Chen Tzu-Yung et al. reported a series of 74 patients with a traumatic epidural hematoma and a Glasgow Coma Scale score of greater than 12， managed nonoperatively； 14 subsequent-ly underwent surgical evacuation. They reported that only su-pratentorial EDH with volume more than 30 ml， a thickness more than 15 mm， and a midline shift more than 5 mmre-quired surgery .

【20】Sullivan et al. reported a large series of 252 consecutive pa-tients with acute epidural hematomas. Overall， 160 of the cases where managed nonsurgically with generally favorable outcomes .

【21】Offner et al. studied 84 patients with epidural hematoma us-ing the Saint Anthony Central Hospital trauma registry. The goal of the study was to compare patients who succeeded or failed nonoperative care to identify risk factors for failure. Overall， 64% of patients in the series were initially treated nonsurgically. Of these， 87% of the nonsurgically treated pa-tients were able to be successfully managed without surgery. However， those who failed nonsurgical management were suc-cessfully treated surgically in a delayed fashion without ad-verse outcome 45.

【22】Bullock et al. suggested criteria for the management of EDH in 2006. They strongly recommended urgent surgical manage ment for patients in coma (GCS score <9) with anisocoria and for those with a hematoma larger than 30 cmin size， regardless of the patient's Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score. Patients with an EDH less than 30 cm3， less than 15-mm in thickness， with less than 5-mm of midline shift， and a GCS score greater than 8without focal deficits were felt to be candidates for nonsurgical management with close observation and serial CT scans .

【23】In the current report， we describe a more severe and well doc-umented epidural hematoma managed conservatively， with a favorable outcome. In our case， the “worst" CT scan demon-strated a maximum thickness of 2.5 cm and 1.2 cm of midline shift. The approximate volume of the hematoma was estimat-ed to be 30 ml. A key point of the current report is that the pa-tient's neurologic examination remained stable throughout the period of observation. To the best of our knowledge， this is one of the few well documented cases of an epidural hematoma of this magnitude managed successfully by nonsurgical care.

【24】Many factors may play a role in the patient’s ability to toler-ate a given clot volume， including rapidity of volume accumu-lation， presence of associated intradural lesions， elasticity of the brain， combined volume of the sulci and other anatomic variations， and the location of the hematoma. EDH， both supra-tentorial and in the posterior fossa， can be managed nonsurgi-cally. A large volume EDH (>30 cm3) can be managed nonsurgi-cally provided the GCS at presentation and follow-up remains the same， with symptomatic improvement .

【25】It can be speculated that in our case not the arterial bleed-ing but the venous one was the driving force of the enlarging EDH. So far studies on influencing factors as age， cerebral at-rophy， the type of the trauma， the relationship of the primary lesion with intra and extra axial vascular structures and gen-eral metabolic parameters are not been published.

【26】Conclusions

【27】This case report is intended to add to the growing knowledge regarding the best management ofthis serious and acute pa-thology. Posttraumatic epidural hematoma presenting a max-imum thickness of 2.5 cm， a midline shift of 1.2 cm， and ap-proximate volume of 30 m. can be successfully managed in a conservative fashion. Further studies on influencing factors must be taken into consideration to allow an updated and more reliable systematization of this complex and challenging issue.

【0】Background：

【1】Aorto-atrial fistulas (AAFs) are rare lesions typically associated with paravalvular abscesses or aortic aneurysms. latrogenic AAFs have been described after cardiac surgery. While these lesions are often asymptomatic， they can cause shunting and volume overload. Diagnosis of AAFs can be challenging. Transesophageal echocardiog-raphy plays a critical role in their diagnosis.

【2】Case Report： A 91-year-old man undergoing transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) for severe aortic stenosis had extreme tortuosity of the aorta and iliofemoral vessels. The patient developed a fistula from the non-sinus of Valsalva to the right atrium during the procedure. After the procedure， the patient developed stroke and ret-roperitoneal hematoma.

【3】Conclusions：

【4】This case represents the first full report of an aorta to right atrial fistula after TAVR. The anatomy of the aor-tic root in relation to the right atrium and ventricle may make aorta to right ventricle fistulas more common than aorta to right atrial fistulas. This patient's vascular tortuosity may have played a role in the development of this lesion. Blood flow in an aorta to right atrial fistula occurs during both systole and diastole， making both right and left ventricle overload possible. Echocardiography is essential to the diagnosis of these lesions. Both vascular injury and landing zone rupture are possible during TAVR， although the observed timing and anatomy of this lesion suggest that it was caused during retrograde access of the left ventricular outflow tract via the ascending aorta.

【5】Keywords： Anatomy ·Aorto-Atrial Tunnel· Transcatheter Aortic Valve Replacement Aorto-atrial fistulas (AAF) are rare lesions connecting the aorta to the cardiac atria. Reports are limited to cases and postmor-tem series， making their true incidence unknown . In adults， AAFs are most often reported as a complication of endocar-ditis with paravalvular abscess， or as a complication of aortic aneurysm and dissection. Fistulas can form between the aor-ta and either atrium， although reports are more frequent with the right atrium (RA) . latrogenic causes of AAF are most of-ten associated with cardiac surgery， including valve replace-ment， saphenous vein graft aneurysm after coronary bypass graft surgery， and atrial septal defect closure AAFs are often asymptomatic， and once AAFs are identified， the patients are observed for clinical deterioration. Larger AAFs can lead to left- to right-sided shunting and volume overload .

【6】The diagnosis and treatment of AAFs can be challenging. AAFs are typically small， and the direction of the shunt can change direction throughout its course， making it difficult to observe the entire course of the lesion via standard echocardiography views . The rarity of this lesion could lead to it being mis-classified as a more common lesion associated with cardiac sur-gery， such as a paravalvular leak. Transesophageal echocardiog-raphy (TEE) plays a key role in the detection of AAFs and has a high sensitivity， owing to the proximity of the esophagus to the atria . AAFs are typically repaired surgically， although transcatheter interventions have also been described . We report an iatrogenic aorta to right atrial fistula that devel-oped during transcatheter aortic valve repair (TAVR).

【7】Case Report

【8】A 91-year-old man with a history of hypertension and former heavy tobacco use presented with shortness of breath and in-ability to perform independent activities of daily living. He had no prior cardiac surgeries or history of anesthetic complica-tions. The physical examination revealed a 3/6 systolic mur-mur that was loudest at the left upper sternal boarder， and the patient was referred for evaluation by transthoracic echocar-diography (TTE). The patient was found to have aortic steno-sis and insufficiency. A TEE was obtained to better character-ize the aortic stenosis prior to the procedure. The patient was found to have severe aortic stenosis， with a calculated aortic valve area of 0.55 cm²， a mean gradient of 30 mm Hg. and a dimensionless index of 0.18. The patient also had aortic in-sufficiency， with a deceleration slope of 248 cm/s2. No aortic insufficiency vena contracta was reported in this study， which was performed at an outside hospital. The patient had a left ventricle (LV) ejection fraction of 60% to 65%， no regional wall motion abnormalities， moderate concentric LV hypertrophy， grade 1 LV diastolic dysfunction， and normal right ventricular (RV) systolic function. Preoperative heart catheterization was challenging owing to extreme tortuosity of the aorta and ilio-femoral vessels. It was not possible to engage the right cor-onary artery at that time， and it was only reported that the circulation was right dominant and that the right coronary ar-tery was grossly patient. Left coronary artery disease was less than 50% occlusive. A preoperative computed tomography an-giogram noted tortuous common and external iliac arteries.

【9】The patient underwent TAVR under monitored anesthesia care. Left femoral and left subclavian access was obtained after we discussed that the previously demonstrated tortuosity of the aorta and iliofemoral arteries could preclude access to the LV outflow tract (LVOT) by femoral access. Tortuosity of the aor-ta and iliofemoral vessels was indeed noted on angiography. Initial attempts to access to the LVOT from wires and catheters placed in the left subclavian artery revealed a waveform characteristic of the RV. Unusual friction was also noted with wire advancement in this position. Generalendo tracheal anesthesia was induced at this time to allow a TEE to be performed to guide the wire and catheter placement. Immediately， a periaortic root hematoma was noted . The patient was observed for 1 h， and the hematoma did not expand. In consideration of the patient's age and frailty， the procedure continued to attempt to stabilize any aortic root in-jury and to avoid surgical intervention on the atrioventricula. Left axillary access was obtained and used to place a 23-mm Edwards Sapien Ultra valve (Edwards Lifescience， Irvine， CA， USA). No paravalvular leak was noted. After deployment of the valve， color Doppler assessment revealed flow from the non-coronary sinus of Valsalva to the RA . Flow through the fistula was noted to be primarily during systole by continu-ous wave Doppler， although some diastolic flow was also likely. The patient was observed for 2 h after deployment of the valve. No other complications arose， and the patient was taken to the Intensive Care Unit (ICU) intubated for recovery.

【10】After arrival in the ICU and weaning of sedation， the patient was noted to have right fascial droop and right hemiplegia.A grade 3 systolic murmur at the left lower sternal boarder， with no rubs， gallops， or thrills， was noted on physical examination at this time. A noncontrast computed tomography scan of the head revealed left middle cerebral artery stoke. The patient was not a candidate for thrombolytic therapy owing to the aor-tic root hematoma. On post-procedural day 1，the patient be-came hypotensive. TEE was negative for tamponade， and the patient was treated with vasoactive infusions. On post-proce-dural day 2， the patient developed anemia and thrombocyto-penia. A computed tomography scan revealed a large， bilater-al retroperitoneal hematoma extending from the level of the kidneys into the pelvis. The patient remained lethargic， with-out improvement of his neurologic symptoms. The patient was extubated in accordance with his wishes on post-procedural day 7 and died shortly after.

【11】Discussion

【12】There is only one other brief report of aorta to right atrial fistula after TAVR that we identified in the literature . Descriptions of ventricular septal defects  and aorta to RV fistulas  seem to be more common. The limitations of using case reports to determine the incidence of a lesion makes it diffi-cult to draw conclusions whether aorta to RV fistulas are more common than aorta to RA fistulas. It may be true that aorta to RA fistulas are less likely to be clinically significant and re-quire surgical or percutaneous intervention， making reports less common. There has been no observational study that de-scribes the incidence of these lesions ， let alone after TAVR. Because these lesions are rare， a very large number of patients would need to be observed to accurately determine incidenc-es. However， given that there were almost 73 000 TAVRs per-formed in the United States in 2019 ， it seems unlikely that repair of these lesions would go unreported ifthey are in fact as common as aorta to RV fistula after TAVR.

【13】The ascending aorta， aortic root， RA， and RV are all in close proximity at the base of the heart. The RV is close to the right coronary sinus of Valsalva， while the RA is closer to the non-coronary sinus of Valsalva . The RV is located apical-ly in relation to the aortic root， while the RA is located basally， seemingly next to rather than above the aortic root. This ori-entation could make aorta to RV fistula formation more like-ly in TAVR than aorta to RA fistula formation. A wire travers-ing the ascending aorta in a retrograde manner would likely be oriented toward the more apically oriented RV rather than the basally oriented RA. Figure 5 shows a white wire placed through the right coronary cusp into the right ventricular out-flow tract， and a red wire placed through the non-coronary cusp into the RA of a pig heart. The red wire requires a much more angulated course to reach the RA than the white wire requires to reach the RV. The angle taken by the red wire re-quires a sharp bend if the more proximal end of the wire is to remain inside of the ascending aorta， which was resected for this dissection. This bend would be unlikely to occur with a wire being pushed from its opposite end. Our particular pa-tient's vascular tortuosity could have allowed an unusual orien-tation of the wire in the ascending aorta that made a straight orientation from the non-coronary sinus of Valsalva to the RA more likely. These anatomic variations and the inability to de-tect them on the procedural fluoroscopy highlight the impor-tance of TEE in the detection and evaluation of AAF in TAVR. similar to previous reports of AAF .

【14】The timing of blood flow in aorta to RA fistulas is important to the clinical manifestations in aorta to RA fistulas. Aortic pres-sure is higher than right atrial pressure in both systole and di-astole. Thus， it would be expected that blood flow through such a fistula would be continuous， with greater flow during systo-le . This pattern was seen in the present case . Systolic flow occurs when the pulmonic valve is open. Thus， it may be expected that left ventricular overload would be more likely to occur. However， the presence of diastolic flow may mean that right-sided overload is also possible in patients with compromised RV systolic function. The presence or ab-sence of shunting and volume overload was key to the deci-sion of whetherto intervene once the fistula was discovered.

【15】The presence of a periaortic hematoma prior to valvuloplasty suggested that an injury occurred during placement of wires and catheters rather than during deployment of the valve. It is possible， however unlikely， that this AAF represented a frac-ture of the aortic annulus or aortic root. Vascular injury and device landing zone rupture are well-known complications of TAVR. Acute uncontained rupture can be fatal and often re-quires emergent surgical intervention with cardiopulmonary bypass. Contained ruptures are more likely to manifest as a paravalvular leak from the aorta into the LVOT. Oversizing the final prosthetic atrioventricular size greater than 120% ofthe initial annulus and a high level of calcification in the LVOT are risk factors for device landing zone rupture .

【16】The transfemoral approach for TAVR is the access route of choice and is associated with superior results . Tortuous ilio-femoral anatomy can preclude the use of the route. TAVR can also be considered via the transaortic， transapical， transcarot-id， and transsubclavian routes .Transaortic and transapical TAVRs require surgical approaches and are associated with high-er mortality than transfemoral approaches . Transcarotid and transsubclavian approaches avoid the need for surgical ac-cess to the thorax . Transaxillary access appears to have im-proved outcomes to surgical nonfemoral approaches and similar outcomes to transfemoral TAVR ， with the possible exceptions of small differences in midterm all-cause mortali-ty  and stroke . These considerations made the trans-subclavian approach an attractive choice for our frail patient with multiple comorbidities who wished for intubation and a long hospital stay. Femoral access was also obtained to facili-tate monitoring and to allow for access， should that route be feasible. It was clear from the initial angiograms that the tortu-osity of the aorta and iliofemoral vessels precluded the use of the transfemoral route for placement of the TAVR valve. Still， the transsubclavian approach is subject to tortuosity in the proxi-mal aorta. The transapical approach may have avoided the pos-sibility of malalignment of the catheters in the ascending aor-ta if this was indeed the cause of the fistula. However， it would have exposed the patient to other complications associated with a surgical approach. It may be reasonable to use TEE to guide wire and catheter placement in patients with tortuous aortas when a transsubclavian approach is selected. This would require utilizing general anesthesia from the start of the case.

【17】Conclusions

【18】Aorta to right atrial fistulas are now known to be a rare com-plication of TAVR，even among the already rare iatrogenic in-tracardiac fistulas. Anatomic relationships likely make aorta to RA fistula uncommon， but aortic tortuosity could make it more likely. The challenges in diagnosing and treating these lesions are likely similar to those of AAF associated with endocardi-tis and surgery. This means that echocardiography likely plays an important role in the detection and evaluation of these le-sions， both during and after TAVR. It may be important to be aware of these rare lesions when diagnosing new abnormali-ties in color flow Doppler after TAVR.

【0】ABSTRACT

【1】Micafungin is an echinocandin-class antifungal agent that is extremely used in the recent era due to minimal toxicity and broad-spectrum activity， unfortunately， has limited ability against Cryptococcus neoformans. Since it’s inherently resistant， indeed disseminated invasive cryptococcosis is becoming an essential issue in echinocandin recipient with impaired immunity. We present a patient with systemic lupus erythematosus and miliary tuberculosis， who developed a fungal infection with invasive cryptococcal fungemia during empirical micafungin therapy. To the best our knowledge， breakthrough disseminated cryptococcosis has not been reported， as seen in our patient. This case highlighted that Cryptococcus neoformans infection should be kept in mind as a possible breakthrough infection while receiving echinocandin， especially in patients with cellular immunodeficiency.

【2】KEYWORDS invasive fungal infection， micafungin， Cryptococcus neoformans

【3】Introduction

【4】Cryptococcus neoformans (C. neoformans) is one of the com-mon opportunistic agents in invasive fungal infection among im-munocompromised patients such as acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS) patients or another impair cell-mediated im-munity host， for example， those receiving immunosuppression， high dose corticosteroid， and chemotherapy . There were a few reports of breakthrough cryptococcal infection during echinocandins therapy occurring in immunocompromised pa-tients. A review of breakthrough invasive mycoses showed that2.4% patients developed non-Candida albicans and aspergillo-sis throughout exposure to echinocandins . On the other side， cases of co-infection with tuberculosis and cryptococcosis are very rarely reported even in patients with impaired cell- mediated immunity . The purpose of this case was to describe a possible case of breakthrough C. neoformans infection during empirical micafungin therapy in systemic lupus erythematosus(SLE) patient on steroid therapy with miliary tuberculosis.

【5】Case Report

【6】A 34-year-old Indonesian female was admitted due to prolonged fever for two weeks. She had a history of  SLE and treated initially with methylprednisolone 1 mg/kg BW for 4 weeks and then maintained with methylprednisolone 16 mg once daily； lung tuberculosis one year earlier and treated with first-line tuberculosis drugs for six months； and  herpes zoster three weeks before admitted. General examination was normal un-less the temperature of 380C. Chest radiology demonstrated widespread small nodular opacities throughout both lungs， pre-sumed to be miliary tuberculosis-laboratory findings described in table 1. SLE treatment with 16 mg methylprednisolone once daily was continued， first-line tuberculosis drugs of isoniazid200 mg/day， rifampicin 450 mg/day， ethambutol 750 mg/day， and pyrazinamide 1，000 mg/day were started. On the 4th day of admission， the patient's condition deteriorated， as she ex-perienced shortness of breath， cough with productive sputum， high fever， nausea and vomiting. Results of the haematological panel were presented in table 1. Blood gas analysis showed pH7.410， pO2 62 mmHg， pCO2 18 mmHg， O2 saturation 93.4%. She was transferred to the intensive care unit with acute respiratory distress syndrome and anuria. Empirical antibiotic therapy of intravenous cefoperazone/ sulbactam of 500 mg/500 mg twice daily was started after aerob micro-organism and fungi cultures for blood， urine， and sputum， and also sputum acid-fast bacilli direct examination were obtained. The cultures showed nega-tive results for bacteria and fungi， but the direct examination of sputum was positive for acid-fast bacilli. Empiric micafungin was started on the 7th day of admission as her condition did not improve despite results of bacteria and fungi cultures.

【9】Re-culture examination was obtained of the 12th day of ad-mission. Unfortunately， the patient demised of the 15th day of admission with sepsis and multiple organ dysfunctions. The result of this culture came out after the patient’s demise and re-vealed C. neoformans  for blood and Stenotrophomonas maltophilia for sputum. Species differentiation and antimicro-bial susceptibility testing were performed by an automated method from VITEX-2 Compact (Biomerieux， France). The min-imum inhibitory concentrations (MICs) and susceptibility for those fungi were 4 ug/mL for fluconazole，1 ug/mL for am-photericin B， <1 ug/mL for 5-flucytosine， and no result for micafungin.

【10】Discussion

【11】C. neoformans is an opportunistic mycosis agent that causes life-threatening infections in immunocompromised populations that caused high morbidity and mortality to affected patients. A review found that the overall hospital mortality rate of56.1%， with no significant difference between patients receiving antifungal agents vs. untreated (56.9% vs.54.8%，p=0.86). In other side， autoimmune disease was an independent risk factor for cryptococcal fungemia (adjusted OR =9.3，%CI1.1-135.7l，p=0.038). This finding illustrated that the functional impairment of T helper cells in SLE played a role as a risk factor for cryptococcal fungemia and mortality . Prolonged and high dose therapy of corticosteroids was also known as a risk factor for cryptococcal fungemia . Another review also found that invasive fungi such as Cryptococcus spp.， Aspergillus spp.and Candida spp. were associated to early-stage SLE disease that used high-dose corticosteroid therapy with a mortality rate of53%.

【12】Fungal bloodstream infections were infrequent as a study in Mexico City found that positive blood culture-based diagnosis was only 11% of cases with C. neoformans identified in 21.2%of cases as the third most commonly found fungi after Candida spp. (43.9%) and Histoplasma capsulatum (27.3%). Similarly with the previous study in Thailand that was found in 14.1% of cases . The empirical choice of antifungal therapy should be based on a host’s susceptibility to specific fungal pathogens. The best antifungal therapeutic strategy against C. neoformans is limited to single or in the combination of amphotericin B (and its liposomal derivatives)， 5-fluorocytosine and azole agents . Although the fungicidal combination is recommended， azole agents， such as fluconazole or voriconazole， is the most reason-able in countries with a high incidence of cryptococcosis . This is related to the unavailability of 5-flucytosine， and the toxicity and need for clinical and laboratory monitoring for amphotericin B . Emerging resistance to antifungal drugs has been re-ported， as a study showed increased fluconazole resistance with 0.6% isolates had MICs of 216 ug/ml . These MICs were comparable to 4% of C. neoformans isolates from a study in Tai-wan . Whilst other studies concluded that there no changes in susceptibility for the past 15 years， although fluconazole is widely used globally . MICs testing using the microdi-lution method from the European Committee on Antibiotics Susceptibility Testing (EUCAST) and the Clinical Laboratory Standards Institute (CLSI) are the gold standard to determine antifungal susceptibility for Cryptococcus . Therefore， the thorough understanding and epidemiological perspective of this disease would be helpful in the prompt diagnosis and therapeu-tic strategies.

【13】It is reasonable to suspect that cryptococcal fungemia in this patient was acquired from colonization or contamination of the central venous catheter (CVC). However， CVC-related fungemia due to C. neoformans was infrequent， and only C. laurentii and Candida parapsilosis fungemia have been documented. It's affil-iated to config ure biofilm on the surface of medical equipment and polystyrene plates. The formation of fungal biofilms de-pends on the supporting surface characteristics as well as growth in the biofilm phase making the fungal cells less vulnerable to potential environmental pressures， including antimicrobials . Other possibility was the reactivation of dormant crypto-coccal lung lesions as consequences of impaired cell-mediated immunity enhanced by corticosteroid immunosuppressive ther-apy. Tuberculosis and cryptococcosis co-infection only a few cases had been reported even in patients with impaired cell-mediated immunity . In addition， only two reports have been published in wherein the clinical presentation of C. neofor-mans was a breakthrough invasive disseminated cryptococcosis.

【14】The echinocandins are the latest antifungal drugs in clinical therapy， which act as non-competitive inhibitors of 3-1，3-glucan synthase， a major structural component of the fungal cell wall. The drugs in this class are caspofungin， micafungin and anidu-lafungin. It is known that echinocandins have a good fungicidal activity against most Candida species and fungistatic activity for Aspergillus species， but unfortunately less effective against C. neoformans， Zygomycetes， Fusarium or Scedosporium. The FKS genes encoded p-1，3-glucan synthases in different fungal species. Echinocandin resistance has been attributed to specific mutations leading to amino acid substitutions in two different regions of these genes (Hot spot 1 and 2 or HS1 and HS2) that caused decreased affinity to the target in fungal cell wall. Crypto-coccus neoformans is inherently resistant to echinocandins . Although content of glucan in C. neoformans cell wall is low， it has a single Fks1 gene that is essential for viability. The amino acid Leu538 of HS1 in C. neoformans Fks1 is substituted with phenylalanine， but the substitution at the homologous position in S. cerevisiae Fks1 had no effect of the echinocandin sensi-tivity . Many studies found that p-1，3-glucan synthase activity of C. neoformans was very sensitive to caspofungin . A recent study found that the CDC50 gene encoding the B-subunit of lipid flippase， a protein that regulates the asymmet-rical orientation of membrane lipids， could be responsible for C. neoformans resistance to caspofungin. Other study found that C. neoformans was sensitized to micafungin by introduc-ing a mutation in some of the ERG genes encoding ergosterol biosynthesis pathways enzymes， then recovered its resistance to micafungin. However， both these findings only moderately increased sensitivity to echinocandins. Thus the C. neoformans mechanism of resistance to echinocandins is not related to the target enzyme insensitivity or enzyme activity. Resistance is likely due to common microbial drug resistance mechanisms， i.e. the B-1，3-glucan synthase resistance to caspofungin； caspo-fungin is excluded from cells， and the target by ATP-binding cassette (ABC) transporters or other mechanisms； or caspofun-gin is degraded either extra- and/or intracellularly .

【15】One study discovered that C. neoformans reshapes cell wall and capsule composition during infection to produce titan cell. It was presumed that this phenomenon likely is the mechanism to escape recognition by， and allow modulation of， the host im-mune system as well as resistance to echinocandins. A study in mice found that there were morphology changes in the initiation and maintenance of C. neoformans infections. During infection， its cell had variable cell body size and capsule size. These struc-tural and morphological characteristics allow C. neoformans to evade and modulate the host immune system As C. neoformans inhaled into the lungs， it differentiates into cells with different size and morphology， including the production of large titan cells .

【16】The cell wall of C. neoformans is composed of a- and β-glucans which are polysaccharides of glucose monomers. The 我-glucans are essential for capsule attachment to the C. neoformans cell body. Disruption of a-1，3-glucan production produces cells that shed capsule material into the environment and lack the surface capsule normally attached to the cell body . Titan cells have a thick and highly cross-linked capsule attached to their cell wall . Thus， the reduction of glucose content of the titan cell wall is unlikely due to decreased of x-glucans as capsule attachment appears to be unaffected.

【17】The cell wall of C. neoformans also contains two types of P-glucans； B-1，3-glucans and p-1，6-glucans. The proportion of each B-glucan type varied on the cryptococcal strain， growth condition， and exposure to caspofungin . The specific func-tion of B-1，6-glucan in the C. neoformans cell wall is not well understood， but disruption of its production results in enlarged， more diffuse， and more permeable capsules than wild type cells. In vivo titan cells have large cross-linked capsules with reduced permeability， suggesting that p-1，6-glucans are either unaffected or increased . The p-glucans are recognized by the Dectin-1 receptor of host immune cells. The low level of glu-can in cell walls and a thick capsule reduce the surface exposure of B-glucans on in vivo C. neoformans cells， thus enabling the Dectin-1 receptor to make direct contact with B-glucans. Direct contact between the Dectin-1 receptor and the microbial surface is required for the activation of the receptor and subsequent signalling . The low level of glucan in cell walls could also explain why echinocandins'effect onB-1，3-glucan synthase does not disrupt the cell walls. During infection， titan cells confer protection from phagocytosis to the entire cryptococcal popu-lation . A large amount of mannose was detected in the titan cell wall， and it could be components of cell wall mannans， mannoproteins， or capsule components trapped in the cell wall during extraction. Mannoproteins located in the inner layer of the C. neoformans cell wall are non-structural cell wall compo-nents that will migrate to the cell surface and secreted into the environment. It was proposed that the increased production of specific mannoproteins could protect from phagocytosis . Previous studies of capsule structure of C. neoformans on differ-ent anatomical location showed differences in capsule structure of cells grown in vitro and those isolated from the lungs， spleen， kidney，liver， heart and brain of infected mice .

【0】ABSTRACT It is presumed that 5.2 percent of the global population between the ages of 15 and 64 years used an illicit drug in 2014. Although dependence is accepted in the current classification International Classification of Diseases(ICD-10)， owing to the physiological drug response， addiction， defined as compulsive drug-seeking and use， maybe more applicable in other circumstances. Regular consumption of drugs causes persistent changes in the brain structures(neuroadaptation) that explain the shift from voluntary drug use to non-voluntary， and therefore， compulsive drug use. Compulsive consumption behaviour relies， in a psychologically way， on the positive reinforcement due to the seeking pleasure and the continuous gratification in this matter. Positive reinforcement is associated with learning with his molecular biological mechanism-neuronal plasticity at the hippocampus.

【1】The neurobiology of addiction consists of the three-stage addiction cycle： binge/intoxication， preoccupation/anticipation and withdrawal/ negative affect. This is reinforced by multiple neuroadaptations in three conforming domains：  increased incentive salience，  decreased brain reward and increased stress，  compromised executive function； and in three chief neurocircuits： basal ganglia， extended amygdala， and prefrontal cortex.

【2】There are a series of neurotransmitters and neuromodulators that are implicated in the complex mechanisms of addiction. Dopamine intervenes in the reward effects of the drugs and the conditioning and memory mechanisms resulting in drug cravings and compulsive drug. Negative reinforcement， the negative emotional state of withdrawal is intermediated by stress-related neurotransmitters， particularly corticotropin-releasing factor (CRF) and dynorphin. Norepinephrine systems in the extended amygdala act in the negative motivational state.

【3】Introduction

【4】Substance use disorders (SUD) incorporate a heterogeneous group of clinical conditions. Partly， this diversity is owed to challenges in defining the disorder that comes with drug abuse. Apart from the contribution of criteria other than medical (e.g. legal， cultural) in determining the normative drug-pertaining be-haviour， the SUD phenotype has not been uniformly described， and there has been disagreement as to what it ought to be con-sidered，e.g.， dependence or addiction . While dependence is accepted in the current psychiatric classification -International Classification of Diseases - 10 (ICD-10)， owing to the physio-logical drug response， addiction， defined as compulsive drug-seeking and use， may be more applicable.

【5】Although addiction is a medical/psychiatric disorder， its basis comes from voluntary norm-violating actions and thus there is a constant moral judgment (especially coming from the society) when it comes to addiction， regardless of the term used. As an interesting piece of trivia， "addictus" was a term used in ancient Rome for a person in a legal slave-like state (for delinquent debt， which， if left unpaid in 30 days， would result in slavery and possibly death) . Today， we can say that addicts are somehow "slaves" to their unusual and bad habits.

【6】Substance addiction remains a substantial and growing pub-lic health problem； in 2017， 19.7 million people age 12 or older in the United States were assessed to have a substance abuse dis-order related to alcohol or illicit drug use. This value comprises14.5 million people with an alcohol use disorder (AUD) and 7.5million people with a substance use disorder (SUD)， the most common illicit drug being marijuana . It is presumed that5.2 percent of the global population between the ages of 15 and64 years (over 360 million people) used an illicit drug in 2014. That signifies an increase of 24 million people since 1990.  Treatment possibilities are often incomplete and suboptimal，and relapses are common. When abstaining from drugs，symptoms of distress and robust cravings to use the substance again may develop and become mainly salient.

【7】The paths leading to addiction are intricate and multifaceted. They comprise differences in molecular and genetic expression， altered brain sensitivities to reward-and stress-related cues，and behavioural patterns that include risk-taking， social isolation， and/or stress dysregulation.

【8】Addiction - is it choice or is it a compulsion?

【9】The etiopathogenesis of substance use disorders has long been divided the medical model， which sees addiction as a disease characterized by compulsive and relapsing drug use over which the addict has little or no control， and the moral model which sees addiction as a choice characterized by voluntary behaviour which the addict can freely control. The medical model is sus-tained by the evidence showing that regular consumption of drugs causes persistent changes in the brain structures and func-tions known to be involved in the motivation of behaviour (with prolonged consumption there is a shift from voluntary， chosen drug use to non-voluntary， and therefore compulsive drug use).

【10】One of the first arguments for compulsion is the fact that addicts regularly and systematically fail to take advantage of alternatives to drugs despite negative consequences for them-selves， and often in spite of what they judge to be the most treasured course of action . There is a propensity for addicts to thoroughly ignore or soften the costs of using drugs while greatly embroidering its profits .

【11】Where things tend to become tragic is the fact that there is plenty of evidence that addicts often continue to seek and take drugs even when no pleasure can be obtained， even in the absence of withdrawal， and even when they are convinced that continuing to use drugs is a catastrophic course of action for them . Addicts， this would suggest， will often continue to judge that abstaining is the best course of action even when they are continuing their drug-oriented behaviour.

【12】As a general definition， drug addiction is a chronically relaps-ing disorder characterized by (a) compulsion to seek and use the drug， (b) loss of control in restraining intake， and (c) appearance of a negative emotional state (e.g.， dysphoria， anxiety irritabil-ity)， which constitutes the motivational withdrawal syndrome when access to the drug is prevented J.

【13】Drug addiction has been conceptualized as a disorder that involves elements of both impulsivity and compulsivity， from which we can imagine a composite addiction cycle comprised of three stages - binge/intoxication， preoccupation/anticipation， and withdrawal/negative affect -where impulsivity often domi-nates at the early stages. Compulsivity comes second， at terminal stages. When the individual shifts from impulsivity to compul-sivity， a change occurs from positive reinforcement driving the motivated behaviour to negative reinforcement driving the mo- tivated behaviour These three stages are conceptualized as interacting with each other， becoming more intense， and ul-timately leading to the pathological state known as addiction.

【14】Animal models suggesting compulsivity

【15】Examples that prove the conversion from drug use to drug addic-tion can be found in recent animal models of prolonged access to self-administration intravenous cocaine. Although contested by some authors (who argue that animals tend to differ from humans， especially when it comes to free-will - a characteristic specific to humans) we now know， without any doubt - and with an experience of more than 30 years- that animal studies have face validity， and have long provided plenty of resource-ful information when it comes to substance use disorders and addiction.

【16】To explore the possibility that differential access to intra-venous cocaine self-administration in rats may generate different designs of drug intake， rats were allowed to self-administrate cocaine for 1 or 6 h per day . 1-hour access to intravenous cocaine per session produced low and stable intake. In con-trast， 6-h access to cocaine produced drug intake that gradually escalated over days. When animals were allowed access to dif-ferent doses of cocaine， both controls titrated their cocaine intake. However， the 6-hour rats consistently self-administered almost twice as much cocaine at any dose tested， further suggesting an upward shift in the set point for cocaine reward in the escalated animals . Such increased self-administration independent animals have now been observed with other substances， such as cocaine， methamphetamine， nicotine， heroin， and alcohol .

【17】Allostatic theory of addiction - the dark side of addic-tion

【18】Compulsivity when it comes to addiction can come from several sources， and here we can include enhanced incentive salience， impairment in executive function and engagement of habit func-tion. However， behind all these causes， there is a negative emo-tional state that presumably has a strong impact on compul-sivity. The negative emotional state that drives the negative reinforcement of addiction has been defined as the "dark side"of addiction .

【19】This negative emotional state that comprehends the with-drawal/negative affect stage comprises key motivational ele-ments， such as chronic irritability， malaise， emotional pain， alex-ithymia， dysphoria， and loss of motivation for natural rewards. As dependence and withdrawal start developing， brain stress systems such as CRF， norepinephrine， and dynorphin are re-cruited， producing stress-like predicaments . At the same time， within the motivational circuits of the ventral striatum-extended amygdala， reward function starts to decrease. This combination of reward neurotransmitter function decline and mobilization of anti-reward systems contributes to the negative reinforcement behind the compulsive drug-seeking behaviour and addiction.

【20】This emotional dysregulation starts with the binge and con-secutive acute withdrawal but mandates neuroadaptive transfor-mation that permits rapid "re-addiction"，months or even years after detoxification and abstinence. Therefore， this emotional dysregulation that appears in addicts is more than a homeostatic dysregulation of hedonic function； it also signifies an energetic disruption with the homeostasis of this system that has been termed allostasis.

【21】Allostatic mechanisms have been theorized to be involved in preserving a functioning brain reward system that has sig-nificance for the pathology of addiction J. Two components are conjectured to adjust to challenges to the brain produced by drugs of abuse： overactivation of brain reward transmitters and circuits and recruitment of the brain anti-reward or brain stress systems.

【22】Addiction from a neurobiological standpoint

【23】Much development in the neurobiology of addiction can be found in the three-stage addiction cycle discussed ear-lier： binge/intoxication， preoccupation/anticipation， and with-drawal/ negative affect. This is reinforced by multiple neuroad-aptations in three conforming domains：  increased incentive salience，  decreased brain reward and increased stress， and compromised executive function； and in three chief neurocir-cuits： basal ganglia， extended amygdala， and prefrontal cortex.

【24】The efforts in the neurobiology of addiction have changed with the accent on the mechanisms of acute reward in the binge/intoxication stage extended to contain neuroadaptations that are after drug exposure.These include modulation of executive function structures and mnemonic structures (and being modulated by mnemonic processes) in the preoccupa-tion/ anticipation periods and instruments driving incentive salience， compulsive habits， shortfalls in reward and recruit-ment of stress during the withdrawal/ negative affect stage. The neuro-adaptational modifications that occur in the brain emo-tional systems account for the neurocircuitry variations that are presumed to have a significant part for compulsivity in addic-tion.

【25】Role of dopamine in addiction

【26】Addictive drugs are fundamentally gratifying. They capture the brain's dopamine system to upsurge dopamine concentrations in the nucleus accumbens， a crucial central point for reward neurocircuitry in the brain . While dopamine is essential for the immediate rewarding effects of drugs ， its position in substance use disorders and addiction is still developing. Since the levels of dopamine is an essential aspect of whether a drug will give a rewarding effect or not， the various properties of dopamine receptors are expected to play noteworthy roles. The prefrontal cortex encompasses both dopamine D1 and D2 recep-tors. D2 receptors have an approximately 10- to 100-fold superior affinity for dopamine than D1 receptors and are consequently are stimulated at lower dopamine concentrations. Usually， the prefrontal cortex gets a low level， steady flow of dopamine about a relatively sluggish， the tonic firing of dopamine neurons in the ventral tegmental area (VTA) that project to the cortex. Never-theless， as a reaction to an unpredicted incident， such as a great reward or very apathetic event， dopamine neurons fire much more rapidly.

【27】This phasic firing results in a sudden， yet fleeting， increase in dopamine. The high levels of dopamine attained during phasic firing can， therefore activate D1 receptors and are assumed to be at the origin of dopamine’s full， rewarding effects . Drugs of abuse， principally psychostimulants， imitate the high dopamine levels produced by phasic firing and so activate both D1 and D2receptors .

【28】D1 receptors stimulate both the reward， through pathways moderating the striatum and cortex， and conditioning and mem-ory mechanisms that include the amygdala， medial orbitofrontal cortex (OFC) and hippocampus. The conditioning/memory processes crucial to addiction permit individuals to associate a stimulus with a reward or reprimand routinely. Possibly un-expectedly， several studies have shown that addictive drugs fail to increase dopamine levels in addicted people in compari-son to nonaddicted controls. Methylphenidate (MPH) did not meaningfully raise dopamine concentrations among active  or detoxified cocaine addicts； cocaine users are also reporting less of a high produced by MPH than controls J. But，among active addicts shown a video to provide craving， high levels of dopamine were present in the dorsal striatum. The scale of this dopamine rise was linked to the degree of drug craving. This advocates that in addition， there is a shift from the drug itself， starting dopamine increase to drug cues and stim-uli initiating dopamine increase. This change from reward to conditioning involves dopamine phasic firing resulting in drug cravings and compulsive drug use in response to drug and other conditioned cues .

【29】Typically， D2 receptors moderate the effects of D1 receptors via the striatal indirect pathway ； then again， quite a lot of studies have exposed that addicted subjects have less dopamine D2 receptors . Decreases in D2 receptors amongst addicted patients are connected to diminished activity in the OFC，ante-rior cingulate gyrus， and dorsolateral prefrontal cortex areas of the brain， which are known to be implicated in emotion regulation and decision making. Because destructions in the orbitofrontal and anterior cingulate cortices are connected to compulsive behaviours， weakened dopamine signalling in these parts in addicted individuals are presumed to be partly account able for compulsive behaviour and impulsivity . In animal studies， amplified dopamine D2 receptor expression in the nu-cleus accumbens reduced drug consumption in models of both alcohol and cocaine dependence .

【30】Role of corticotropin-releasing factor and dynorphin

【31】The brain's reward and stress systems are knottily connected. Extreme instigation of the reward system， as in the case of exces-sive drug use， can also activate the brain's stress system； addicts can therefore lose regular function of aspects of their reward systems， as well as increased activation of their stress system.

【32】George Koob expressed his long-lasting appeal to under-standing the networks between stress and addiction and how they contribute to a powerful supplementary basis of motiva-tion in addiction： negative reinforcement. Here， Koob claims that the driving energy for negative reinforcement is the neg-ative emotional state of withdrawal intermediated by stress related neurotransmitters， particularly corticotropin-releasing factor (CRF) and dynorphin. He highlighted that numerous other stress-related neurotransmitters could change concentra-tions in addiction that require further study . During acute stress， the peptide CRF is activated in the extended amygdala during withdrawal from abused substances that include alcohol， cocaine ， cannabinoids ， opioids ， and nicotine. CRF antagonists decrease withdrawal-induced anxiety-like responses in animals  and decrease alcohol consumption in alcohol-dependent rats while having zero effect on alcohol ingestion in non-dependent rats .

【33】These dynamic variations in extrahypothalamic CRF may begin with the initial hormonal response of augmented release of glucocorticoids determined by hypothalamic CRF. Similar to CRF antagonists， glucocorticoid antagonists reduced alco-hol ingesting in alcohol-dependent animals， but not that non-dependent . A recent human study for alcohol addiction proved that the glucocorticoid antagonist mifepristone reduced craving and drinking compared with placebo .

【34】Dynorphin is a kappa opioid that can be moderated by activa-tion of dopamine or opioid receptors . Distinct than other opi-oids， kappa opioids give moods of dysphoria. Compulsive drug-taking increases dynorphin levels in the nucleus accumbens and amygdala， causative for a dysphoric-like state. Elevated levels of dynorphin indicate through a negative feedback loop to stop dopamine release， and kappa opioid agonists lower extracel-lular dopamine concentrations in the nucleus accumbens . The kappa antagonist norbinaltorphimine (nor-BNI) reduces extreme drinking in alcohol-dependent rats， with no effect in non-dependent controls， much more like CRF and glucocorticoid antagonists . Injecting nor-BNI into dynorphin-expressing areas of the nucleus accumbens blocks withdrawal-induced rises in alcohol ingestion in rats .

【35】Role of norepinephrine and neuropeptide I

【36】Though less established， an indication exists for the role of nore-pinephrine systems in the extended amygdala in the negative motivational state. Norepinephrine-functional antagonists (β1antagonist and a2 agonist) injected into the lateral bed nucleus of the stria terminalis stopped precipitated opiate withdrawal-induced place aversions . The effects of norepinephrine in intermediating the motivational effects of opioid withdrawal contain the ventral noradrenergic system. Norepinephrine an-tagonists stop extreme drug intake associated with dependence on ethanol ， cocaine ， and opioids . A focal place for many of these influences is the extended amygdala but at the level of the bed nucleus of the stria terminalis.

【37】Hypothesized as a feed-forward system at several levels of the pons and basal forebrain， CRF stimulates norepinephrine， while norepinephrine stimulates CRF . Much pharmacologic， physiologic， and anatomic evidence supports an essential role for a CRF-norepinephrine interface in the locus coeruleus in reply to stressors . However， norepinephrine also excites CRF release in the central nucleus of the amygdala， the bed nucleus of the stria terminalis and the paraventricular nucleus of the hypothalamus .

【38】Neuropeptide Y (NPY) is a neuropeptide with excellent anxiolytic-like properties found in the amygdala and has been theorized to have contrary effects to CRF in the negative motiva-tional state of withdrawal . Plenty of evidence advocates that activation of NPY in the central nucleus of the amygdala can stop the motivational aspects of dependence associated with chronic ethanol consumption. NPY administered intracerebroventricu-larly blocked the increased drug intake associated with ethanol dependence . Injection of NPY directly into the central nu-cleus of the amygdala  and viral vector-enhanced expression of NPY in the central nucleus of the amygdala also blocked the increased drug intake associated with ethanol dependence .

【39】Learning mechanisms underlying addiction

【40】Based on the overhead deliberations， we suggest that conversion to addiction is comprised of three phases： The first phase is recre-ational use. Drug use is sporadic and occupies a small portion of the addict's behaviour. The second phase is the intensified and sustained drug use， which starts with growth in regularity， quantity， and incentive to take drugs. Drug consumption inten-sifies， thus becoming sustained； also， the addict can begin to experience drug-related symtoms but they are not grave enough to endorse self-restraint. The final phase represents the begin-ning of the most serious pathological state and is called loss of control， in which the user can now be described as addicted. Social degradation is unavoidable， and relapses to addiction， even with extended periods of abstinence， is the law.

【41】It is important to highlight that throughout the transition to addiction， drug use first changes quantitatively (from recre-ational to sustained) and then qualitatively (from sustained to loss of control).

【42】Founded on experimental data， two main theoretical bases have been proposed to explain the transition to addiction： drug-centred and individual-centred theories. These two clusters of theories were primarily derivative from two mutual clinical remarks： the first one being that evolution to addiction happens just after lengthy drug use (drug centred)， and the second one is that shift to addiction is detected solely in a restricted number of drug users (individual-centred).

【43】Addiction： drugs or individuals?

【44】Drug-centred theories

【45】Bestowing to these theories， addiction derives from the psy-chopharmacological deviations that derive from chronic drug use. Theories regarding this group focused on specific drug-induced changes， such as tolerance ， sensitization ， with-drawal and allostasis  or drug-induced cognitive changes in impulsivity ， decision making ， and conditioning .

【46】Individual-centered theories

【47】Individual-centered theories of addiction are primarily enthused by observations in humans， which are well summarized by Charles P. O'Brien， who stated： "Some addicts go for months or years using heroin or cocaine only on weekends before be-coming a daily (addicted) user. Others report that they had such an intense positive response that they became addicted with the first dose." . For this group of theories， drugs are essential but not satisfactory enough to the development of addiction. Conferring to this theory， addiction results from a pathological response to the drug that is generated in a few individuals by a vulnerable biological phenotype. Several exper-imental observations reinforce the supposition of the existence of a drug-vulnerable phenotype .

【48】Research in laboratory animals over the last 20 years has increasingly established that individual vulnerabilities to drugs do exist and are originate from the biological factors that mediate transition to addiction， being an obligatory condition for the shift to addiction. Transition to addiction is not facilitated by not one， but two distinct vulnerable phenotypes： the first phenotype promotes drug escalation and the shift to the sustained phase， the second triggers the evolution to the loss of control phase . This explains why just a minor number of people exposed to drugs progress to the most severe form of the disease.

【49】Drug cue-induced neuroplasticity is associated with full addiction

【50】When an addict comes across an external cue or stimulus related to a drug， cells in the nucleus accumbens are triggered， ensu-ing a cue-specific engram that results in drug-seeking behavior.

【51】In controls without addiction， competing judgements or cues can adjust that retort. Nevertheless， drug cues leave behind long-term potentiation of activity of the nucleus accumbens that diminishes the effects of opposing stimuli .

【52】Michael Scofield has best described the mechanism behind this. Usually， when a cue arrives to the prefrontal cortex，gluta-mate is discharged into the nucleus accumbens， stimulating a small percentage of neurons， ensuing a stimulus-specific mem-ory trace or engram. Excess glutamate is taken out from the synaptic cleft by transporters including GLT-1， a glutamate trans-porter originating on astroglial cells. However， looking at animal models of drug addiction， the theory is that GLT-1 is downreg ulated， and there are less astroglial cells in the synaptic cleft.

【53】1Therefore， drug cues cause the buildup of glutamate in the synaptic cleft； consequent activation of mGluR5， a receptor found on interneurons that express neuronal nitric oxide syn-thase； release of nitric oxide into the extracellular space； nitro-sylation； and activation of matrix metalloproteases (MMPs)， es-pecially MMP9， that cause local degradation of the extracellular matrix. This succession of actions delivers transient plastic-ity that contributes to drug-seeking behaviour. In withdrawn animals， drug cues produce considerable increases in MMP9. Inhibiting MMP9 prevents drug-seeking behaviour in reply to drug-associated cues .

【54】Downregulation of GLT-1 can be found with the adminis-tration of several addictive substances to animals， including cocaine ， nicotine ， heroin ， and alcohol . Accu-mulation of glutamate has been observed in animal models of cocaine ， nicotine ， alcohol  and methamphetamine addictions . Drugs that augments GLT-1 function， includ-ing N-acetylcysteine (NAC)， Ceftriaxone， and propentofylline， have revealed optimistic results in animal models of addiction to cocaine ， nicotine  and alcohol  use disorders.

【55】Goal-directed vs habitual behaviour-a likely road to full addiction

【56】One thought-provoking supposition advanced lately is that dur-aling SuDPos ing evolution to addiction， changes in synaptic plasticity migrate following a ventrodorsal gradient )\]. Variations in plasticity would occur rapidly in the VTA， move then to the accumbens， and lastly on to the prefrontal cortex. Thus， the accumbens looks to be entirely safe during the first week of self-administration， during which the VTA should be affected. Alterations in the accumbens appear only later on but before the development of addiction-like behaviours. Thelast structure to present modifi-cations in synaptic plasticity (which appears only in addicted controls) is the prefrontal cortex .

【57】While regions like the basolateral amygdala and nucleus accumbens are necessary to develop prolonged drug-seeking behaviour ， they turn out to be not as much as significant after the behaviour has been developed. Then， the dorsolateral striatum plays a much more vital role . In rats involved in long-term drug-seeking behaviour， a great rise in dopamine is detected in the dorsal striatum， but not in the nucleus ac-cumbens core or shell . Blocking dopamine receptors in the dorsal striatum， but not the nucleus accumbens core， reduced well-known， habitual drug-seeking behaviour . When ac-tions switch from goal-directed to habitual， there is a matching change from the ventral to the dorsal striatum. Disengaging the ventral and dorsal striata reduced cocaine-seeking actions in rats， signifying that there is a linking between the two systems

【58】Conclusion

【59】Although there is much information yet to come in the field of addiction， most theories affirm that addiction is a truly psychi-atric disease and should be treated as such. Though it starts as a volitional activity， it then- due to changes in neurobiology and individual vulnerabilities-switches to a compulsion， in which the addict becomes a"slave" to his habits. Further research is needed (perhaps more in the field of genomics) to understand addiction fully and to prescribe the best appropriate treatment.

【0】Background：

【1】Wegener’s granulomatosis (WG) is a granulomatous vasculitis that in typical course involves both the upper respiratory tract and the lung， along with a non-granulomatous necrotizing glomerulonephritis. Immune dysfunction in patients with Wegener's granulotnatosis and immunosuppressive regimen may predispose to recurrent infections.

【2】Case report：

【3】We report on a 61-year-old man with WG and renal failure， who experienced 4 times recurrent Salmonella sepsis with positive blood， urine， stool cultures and septic hip arthritis， which made him bed-ridden. The patient improved after combined high dose (according to renal failure) ciprofloxacin (0，8 g/d i.v.) and ceftriaxone (4g/d i.v.) for over 20 days plus cholecystectomy.

【4】Conclusions：

【5】Successful treatment of recurrent salmonellosis in an immunocompromised patient is based on diligent searching for persistent Salmonella focuses， and prolonged antibiotic treatment.

【6】Key words：

【7】renal failure· recurrent salmonella infection · Wegener’s granulomatosis · septic arthritis·gallbladder Immune dysfunction in patients with Wegener’s granulomatosis (WG) may predispose to recurrent infections. In those patients， reduced CD4-CD8T cell ratios resulting from primary disease as well as therapeutic immunosuppression may be the most likely risk factors for recurrent nontyphoidal salmo-nellosis .

【8】We report an unusual case of a WG patient who ex-perienced recurrent Salmonella sepsis for 4 times with positive blood， urine and stool cultures and septic hip arthritis， which made him bed-ridden.

【9】CASE REPORT

【10】A 61-year-old man was diagnosed in June 2002 as suffering from Wegener’s granulomatosis with renal involvement. The titer of cytoplasmic antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (C-ANCA) was 135，5 IU at the time of diagnosis. Other laboratory tests showed the following abnormalities： ESR 160 mm/h， haemoglobin8，8 g/dl， platelets 421000/l， C-reactive proteine (CRP)53，7 mg/l， albumin 27 g/l， serum creatinine 8，5 mg/dl， BUN 41 mmol/l. Chest X-rays were normal except for calcifications in the right upper lobe probably after tuberculosis (positive history of pulmonary tubercu-losis). Abdominal ultrasound revealed 24 mm cyst in right kidney. Due to high disease activity and renal insufficiency immunosuppressive therapy (i.v. cyclo-phosphamide in combination with prednisone)and haemodialysis were started. An improvement in renal function (serum creatinine 3，3 mg/dl) enabled discon-tinuation of haemodialysies after one month.

【11】Two months later he was readmitted to the hospital because of pneumonia， fever， pain in the left thigh， left knee and renal function impairment (serum cre-atinine 4，1 mg/dl)， while under treatment with pred-nisone 50 mg/d. A kidney oligobiopsy was performed and showed diffuse chronic glomerulonephritis； ad-vanced stage of fibrosis with seven fibrotic glomeruli. Advanced involutional changes in the biopsy and low c-ANCA titer forced us to stop cyclophosphamide， to reduce prednisone dose and to carry out further investigations based on differential diagnosis. The urine and blood cultures revealed Salmonella species； stool culture indicated Salmonella typhimurium. The occurrence of bacteremia was not associated with gastrointestinal symptoms. Majority of symptoms resolved on treatment with a second generation cephalosporin (5 days i.v.) and ciprofloxacin (7 days i.v. plus 7 days p.o.). After the treatment， all cultures were negative and serum creatinine decreased to3，6 mg/dl.

【12】Five weeks later， he developed a second episode of septic salmonellosis with fever and painful left thigh. Due to WG， patient was given prednisone 25mg/d. Laboratory investigations showed low WG activity： ANCA <8 IU； ESR 50 mm/h， CRP 38 mg/l and stable renal function： serum creatinine 3，8-3，1mg/dl， BUN 22 mmol/l. Blood cultures were posi-tive for S. typhimurium. The isolate was susceptible to penicillins， caphalosporins， quinolones and tri-methoprim-sulfamethoxazol (TMP-SMZ). He was treated with ampicillin (7 days i.v.)， ciprofloxacin(11 days i.v. plus 7 days p.o.) plus TMP-SMZ (16 days p.o.)， which resulted in clinical improvement.

【13】The third recurrence of salmonellosis occured in February 2003. At that time he was on treatment with prednisone 20 mg/d. Salmonella typhimurium was found in urine and stool. There was no evidence of osteomyelitis， cholecystitis or other focus of infec-tion. No evidence of clinical or immunological WG exacerbation was noted. Antibiotic treatment with cefuroxime (10 days i.v.) and ciprofloxacin (10 days i.v. and 6weeks p.o.) was initiated and the symptoms resolved.

【14】The patient was readmitted to the hospital in September 2003 because of deterioration in renal function， pain in the left hip region which disabled his walking but without gastrointestinal symptoms. He was on treatment with prednisone 15 mg/d at the time. On physical examination， he had fever of 37.8C， blood pressure 110/70， with normal heart， lungs and abdomen findings， painful palpable masses in both groins and limitation of movement of the left hip joint. Laboratory tests showed the following： ESR 64mm/h， CRP 65 mg/l， WBC count 10000/l， haemoglo-bin 11，1 g/dl， platelets 334000/l， serum creatinine 3，7mg/dl， BUN 33 mmol/l， albumin 35 g/dl， c-ANCA titer9，7 IU. Screening test for HIV was negative. Urine cultures revealed S. typhimurium but blood and stool cultures were negative. The isolate was susceptible to penicillins， cephalosporins， quinolones and mac-rolides. Chest X-rays were comparable to previous ones (at the time of diagnosis). Contrast intestinal radiographs did not show anatomic abnormalities such as diverticulosis which could serve as focus of infection. Ultrasound of the left groin showed fluid space in cystic form extending from the hip to the left upper tight. Puncture of this space revealed 120 ml of inflammatory fluid. Abdominal sonography showed：a 20 mm cyst in the right kidney and an echodense mass in the gallbladder， which was moving as patient was changing position together with incrustation of the gallbladder walls . These changes in the gallbladder were not seen in abdominal sonography before.

【15】Despite high doses of antibiotics (ceftriaxone 4g/d i.v.- 20 days plus ciprofloxacin 0，8g/d i.v.-14 days) only slight clinical improvement was observed. Due to highly suspected Salmonella reservoir in the gall-bladder we decided to perform cholecystectomy. Laparoscopic cholecystectomy was carried out in order to save the peritoneum for the possible renal replacement therapy in the future. Antibiotic treat-ment was continuated after the surgery (addition-ally ceftriaxone 4g/d i.v. -20 days plus ciprofloxacin0，8g/di.v. -20 days) and significant clinical remission of salmonellosis was observed. Serum creatinine de-creased to 2，8 mg/dl and is stable until today. The patient was able to walk again.

【16】DISCUSSION

【17】About one-third of the patients with WG develop a serious infection during follow-up， and older patients are at highest risk. Lymphopenic patients， mainly lacking CD4 T-cells， seem to be at particular risk too. Most common infectious agents identified in patients with Wegener's granulomatosis with renal involvement are Pneumocystis carini， Varicella-zoster virus， Streptococcus pneumoniae， StraphylococCuS 鐵u- reus， Cytomegalovirus and Gram-negative bacteria， including Salmonella species .

【18】Salmonella can be easily eradicated in healthy in-dyviduals but it causes widespread relapsing infec-tions in immunocompromised patients. Frequently associated conditions include AIDS， haematologic and solid-organ malignancies， haemoglobinopaties， diabetes， liver cirrhosis， immunosupressive therapy， long-term haemodialysis， splenectomy and immu-nodeficiency of other causes . Anatomical disruptions， including kidney stones and other urinary tract abnormalities， gallstones， atheroscle-rotic endovascular lesions and prosthetic devices， may all serve as foci for persistent Salmonella in- fection .

【19】We report the case of S. typhiumurium sepsis relaps-ing 4 times in a patient with WG. There are two rea-sons for immune system impairment in WG： the imbalance of lymphocyte subsets (CD4+ decrease， CD8+57+ increase)， which is similar to that seen in AIDS ；  pharmacologic immunosuppression and the resultant lymphocytopenia， as well as the lymphocyte and monocyte functional abnormalities caused by glucocorticoids. Moreover， gallstones found in our patient were the predisposing factor for persistent Salmonella reservoir.

【20】Intercurrent infection may mimic primary disease flare-up and the differential diagnosis may be dif-ficult. During each recurrence our patient’s labo-ratory investigation showed mild WG activity (low c-ANCA titer)， but renal failure was accelerated. Renal function improved each time after the course of antibiotic.

【21】Although Salmonella gastroenteritis is the most com-mon symptom， bacteremia and various extraintes-tinal Salmonella presentation are not infrequently reported， especially in immunocompromised patients. Recent retrospective review of cases of nontyphoidal Salmonella bacteremia seen at Children’s Hospital in Boston showed that focal infections included men-ingitis， septic arthritis， osteomyelitis， cholangitis and pneumonia. In adults， bacteremia is even more seri-ous， which reflects the persistence of bacteria and other comorbidities. In the United Kingdom， mortality in patients over the age of 60 years with nontyphoidal Salmonella infections was reported up to 28%.小These patients represent a small percentage of large number of people with both overt and subclinical in-testinal infection. In a Spanish study of 172 cases of

【22】Salmonella bacteremia (70% S. enteritidis and 17%

【23】S. typhimurium)， 16% of patients developed septic metastases， and 16% died. Approximately 17% had a relapse after therapy， and nearly 60% of those who had a relapse also had AIDS .

【24】The synovial membranes are particular metastatic focuses of Salmonella bacteremia and can result in disability. Salmonella septic arthritis is usually a blood-borne local infection.

【25】The high frequency of steroid use for systemic dis-ease is an important contributory factor. Salmonella typhimurium induce widespread infection and is considered the most frequent serotype of Salmonella causing septic arthritis. The hip and the knee joint are the most frequently affected joints in patients with SLE and other systemic diseases. There are reports of successful treatment of septic arthritis after combined appropriate surgical intervention and prolonged antibiotics administration . Although the left hip was affected in our patient， radiographs and joint ultrasound did not demonstrate articular destruction. so we did not pursue the surgery option.

【26】Extraintestinal Salmonella isolates in our patient were most frequently found in urine. Positive urine culture results may erroneously be attributed to fecal contamination or “urinary tract colonization"， but they often reflect bacteriemic seeding and secondary infection of the urinary tract. Especially in case of functionally or structurally abnormal urinary tracts， it may be necessary to use longer courses of antimi-crobial agents excreted in the urine (e.g. TMP-SMZ or quinolones) to eradicate infection .

【27】There are no therapeutic standards for patients with recurrent Salmonella sepsis.

【28】Management of chronic fecal carriage of nontyphoi-dal Salmonella species is generalized from experience with S. typhi， and includes the long-term use of anti-biotics and consideration of cholecystectomy .

【29】The antibiotic treatment regimens for our patient’s first to third septicaemia episodes included am-picillin， second generation cephalosporin， cipro-floxacin and TMP-SMZ but were not successful in preventing relapsing sepsis. These antibiotics were reported as highly effective in vitro， but they may have failed in vivo because of limited con-centrations in intracellular compartments where Salmonellas can persist . Additionally， increas-ing resistance to TMP-SMZ and ampicillin were observed. Recent data suggest usage of a third-gen-eration cephalosporins or fluoroquinolones in the treatment of Salmonella infections also in a patient on immunosupression . Standard doses (ac-cording to renal function) of ciprofloxacin (0，4g/d i.v. or 0，5 g/d p.o) or ceftriaxone (2g/d i.v.) seem to be inadequate in treating patients with recurrent salmonellosis. Combined high dose ciprofloxacin(0，8 g/d i.v.) and ceftriaxone (4g/d i.v.) for over 20days plus cholecystectomy was finally successful in eradicating Salmonellas in our patient. Eradication by a combination of high dose ciprofloxacin and ceftriaxone has been reported in an immunode-ficient 33-year woman with recurrent Salmonella enteritidis sepsis .

【30】CONCLUSIONS

【31】The history of our patient demonstrates the clinical importance of Salmonella infection in WG. From the clinical point of view， it should be stressed that successful treatment of recurrent Salmonellosis in an immunocompromised patient is based on a diligent search for and elimination of persis-tent Salmonella focuses， and prolonged antibiotic treatment.

【0】ABSTRACT Introduction： Reactive oxygen species (ROS) are produced continuously in our body as a result of bio-chemical reactions which mav cause oxidative stress and various dysfunctions. Antioxidants are substances which are postulated to prevent or even overcome the adverse effects of free radicals. Glutathione is a type of antioxidant that is required for maintaining mitochondrial function， DNA health， improving immune function and providing anti-inflammatory effects. However， the benefit of glutathione as a health supplement in healthy individuals is yet to be elucidated. Method： A total of 30 healthy women was included in this double-blinded randomized controlled trial study. Subjects were randomly allocated into two groups receiving placebo and antioxidant capsule， respectively. One capsule of antioxidant contains 500 mg L-glutathione， 250 mg ascorbic acid， 50 mg alpha-lipoic acid (ALA)， and 4 mg zinc which was given every day to the treatment group for 12 weeks. The total antioxidant serum (TAS) level before and after 12weeks of treatment was examined using ELISA. Result： No significant TAS level difference was observed between both groups before and after treatment (p>0.05). Also， there was also no significant difference in TAS level within the group before and after 12 weeks of treatment (p>0.05). No significant side effects were observed. Conclusion： This study shows that short-term administration of antioxidant supplement containing glutathione， ascorbic acid， ALA， and zinc did not significantly affect the antioxidant level.

【1】KEYWORDS alpha lipoic acid， glutathione， total antioxidant status， vitamin C，zinc

【2】Introduction

【3】Reactive oxygen species (ROS) are produced continuously in our body as a result of biochemical reactions. If the production of ROS and other free radicals exceeds the capacity of endogenous antioxidants， a condition called oxidative stress would occur. Excessive ROS will damage cellular lipids， proteins and DNA and inhibit normal cell function， which can cause various dis-eases， such as cancer， hypertension， diabetes， atherosclerosis， and premature ageing.

【4】Antioxidants are substances which can inhibit or delay the oxidation of various substrates. Endogenous antioxidant sub-stances consist of non-enzymatic， such as uric acid， glutathione， bilirubin， thiols， albumin， and nutritional factors， including vita-mins and phenols) and enzymatic， such as superoxide dismutase(SOD)， glutathione peroxidases \[GSH-PX\]， catalase， and glu-tathione reductase (GSHR). When antioxidant defences weaken， body cells and tissues become more susceptible to deterioration and disease. Therefore， maintaining antioxidant levels at an adequate level is essential in preventing or even overcoming various types of diseases.， Glutathione is a low molecular weight thiol which has an essential role in maintaining the intracellular redox balance. Glu-tathione is essential for maintaining mitochondrial function， DNA health， and energy production. Also， it is also beneficial in improving immune function and providing anti-inflammatory effects. This is augmented by the fact that healthy subjects are shown to have optimal glutathione levels.

【5】However， the benefit of glutathione given as a health supple-ment in healthy individuals is yet to be elucidated. Most studies were done on subjects with diseases， and to our knowledge， only one study was done in healthy subjects9. This study aims to examine the effect of antioxidant supplementation on the total antioxidant status (TAS) level in healthy subjects.

【6】Methods

【7】Study Design

【8】The double-blinded randomized controlled trial study was con-ducted in the Dermatovenereology Department， Faculty of Medicine， Hasanuddin University from May until July 2018and has obtained approval from the Institutional Ethical Review Board.

【9】Subjects

【10】A total of 30 healthy volunteers aged 30-65 vears old were in-cluded in this study. All patients were healthy subjects. In-formed consent was obtained from each subject. Patients with history or family history with skin cancer chronic systemic dis-ease，supplementation containing glutathione or other antioxi-dants， and smoking were excluded. The sampling method used was consecutive sampling.

【11】Study Protocol

【12】Subjects were randomly allocated into two groups using block randomization method. One capsule of antioxidant containing500 mg L-glutathione， 250 mg ascorbic acid， 50 mg alpha-lipoic acid (ALA)， and 4 mg zinc was given every day to the treat-ment group for 12 weeks. The other group was given a placebo capsule with similar size， shape， and colour for the same du-ration. Venipuncture was done in each subject to measure the total antioxidant serum (TAS) level before and after 12 weeks of treatment. The TAS level examination was carried out using ELISA with human total antioxidant capacity (T-AOC) kit (Bioas-say Technology Laboratory) following the instruction from the manufacturer.

【13】Statistical Analysis

【14】The data in this study were analyzed using the Statistical Pack-age for Social Sciences (SPSS) 21.0 for Windows (SPSS Inc. Chicago， IL， USA). Results were presented in the form of ta-bles and charts. Wilcoxon test was used to compare the median of TAS level in each before and after treatment. The differ-ence of TAS level between both groups was assessed using the Mann-Whitney test. A p-value of less than 0.05 was considered significant.

【15】Results

【16】A total of 30 subjects were included in this study. Most subjects(86.67%) were between 30-45 years old and worked as a cleaning service .
